claim: Subunit vaccines comprised of glycoprotein D (gD-2) failed to prevent HSV-2.
source: Subunit vaccines comprised of glycoprotein D (gD-2) failed to prevent HSV-2 highlighting need for novel strategies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact that motivates the current study.

claim: Subcutaneous immunization of C57BL/6 or BALB/c mice with ΔgD−/+gD1 provided 100% protection against lethal intravaginal challenge.
source: Subcutaneous immunization of C57BL/6 or BALB/c mice with ΔgD−/+gD1 provided 100% protection against lethal intravaginal or skin challenges and prevented latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 3A and 3I showing survival curves.

claim: Subcutaneous immunization of C57BL/6 or BALB/c mice with ΔgD−/+gD1 provided 100% protection against lethal skin challenges.
source: Subcutaneous immunization of C57BL/6 or BALB/c mice with ΔgD−/+gD1 provided 100% protection against lethal intravaginal or skin challenges and prevented latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 4C showing disease scores and survival.

claim: Subcutaneous immunization with ΔgD−/+gD1 prevented latency.
source: Subcutaneous immunization of C57BL/6 or BALB/c mice with ΔgD−/+gD1 provided 100% protection against lethal intravaginal or skin challenges and prevented latency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no viral DNA detected by qPCR and no ex vivo reactivation in vaccinated mice (Figure 3F, 3G, 3H).

claim: ΔgD−/+gD1 elicited no disease in SCID mice.
source: ΔgD−/+gD1 elicited no disease in SCID mice, whereas 1000-fold lower doses of wild-type virus were lethal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing survival of SCID mice inoculated with up to 10^7 pfu of ΔgD−/+gD−1.

claim: 1000-fold lower doses of wild-type virus were lethal in SCID mice compared to ΔgD−/+gD1.
source: ΔgD−/+gD1 elicited no disease in SCID mice, whereas 1000-fold lower doses of wild-type virus were lethal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing that 10^4 pfu of wild-type virus was lethal while 10^7 pfu of ΔgD−/+gD−1 was not.

claim: HSV-specific antibodies were detected in serum at a titer of 1:800,000 following immunization.
source: HSV-specific antibodies were detected in serum (titer 1:800,000) following immunization and in vaginal washes after intravaginal challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6A showing anti-HSV-2 antibody titers.

claim: HSV-specific antibodies were detected in vaginal washes after intravaginal challenge.
source: HSV-specific antibodies were detected in serum (titer 1:800,000) following immunization and in vaginal washes after intravaginal challenge.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6B showing antibody detection in vaginal washes.

claim: The antibodies elicited by ΔgD−/+gD1 had little neutralizing activity.
source: The antibodies elicited cell-mediated cytotoxicity, but little neutralizing activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6C showing low neutralizing activity (1:5 dilution).

claim: The antibodies elicited by ΔgD−/+gD1 elicited cell-mediated cytotoxicity.
source: The antibodies elicited cell-mediated cytotoxicity, but little neutralizing activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6D showing ADCC activity.

claim: Passive transfer of immune serum completely protected wild-type mice.
source: Passive transfer of immune serum completely protected wild-type, but not Fcγ-receptor or neonatal Fc-receptor knock-out mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A and 5C showing 100% survival in wild-type mice receiving immune serum.

claim: Passive transfer of immune serum did not protect Fcγ-receptor knock-out mice.
source: Passive transfer of immune serum completely protected wild-type, but not Fcγ-receptor or neonatal Fc-receptor knock-out mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A showing lack of protection in FcγR−/− mice.

claim: Passive transfer of immune serum did not protect neonatal Fc-receptor knock-out mice.
source: Passive transfer of immune serum completely protected wild-type, but not Fcγ-receptor or neonatal Fc-receptor knock-out mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7B showing lack of protection in FcRn−/− mice.

claim: Non-neutralizing Fc-mediated humoral responses confer protection against HSV-2.
source: These studies demonstrate that non-neutralizing Fc-mediated humoral responses confer protection and support advancement of this attenuated vaccine.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combination of low neutralizing activity (Figure 6C), ADCC activity (Figure 6D), and loss of protection in FcγR and FcRn knockout mice (Figure 7).

claim: Over 500 million people are infected with HSV-2 worldwide.
source: The World Health Organization estimated that over 500 million people are infected with HSV-2 worldwide with approximately 20 million new cases annually (Looker et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Looker et al., 2008.

claim: Approximately 20 million new HSV-2 cases occur annually.
source: The World Health Organization estimated that over 500 million people are infected with HSV-2 worldwide with approximately 20 million new cases annually (Looker et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Looker et al., 2008.

claim: HSV-2 is the leading cause of genital ulcerative disease.
source: HSV serotype 1 (HSV-1) is associated primarily with oral mucocutaneous disease, sporadic encephalitis, and is a leading cause of corneal blindness worldwide, whereas HSV serotype 2 (HSV-2) is the leading cause of genital ulcerative disease and a major cofactor in fueling the HIV epidemic (Gray et al., 2001; Wald and Link, 2002; Freeman et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2001; Wald and Link, 2002; Freeman et al., 2006.

claim: HSV-2 is a major cofactor in fueling the HIV epidemic.
source: HSV serotype 1 (HSV-1) is associated primarily with oral mucocutaneous disease, sporadic encephalitis, and is a leading cause of corneal blindness worldwide, whereas HSV serotype 2 (HSV-2) is the leading cause of genital ulcerative disease and a major cofactor in fueling the HIV epidemic (Gray et al., 2001; Wald and Link, 2002; Freeman et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2001; Wald and Link, 2002; Freeman et al., 2006.

claim: HSV-1 is a leading cause of corneal blindness worldwide.
source: HSV serotype 1 (HSV-1) is associated primarily with oral mucocutaneous disease, sporadic encephalitis, and is a leading cause of corneal blindness worldwide, whereas HSV serotype 2 (HSV-2) is the leading cause of genital ulcerative disease and a major cofactor in fueling the HIV epidemic (Gray et al., 2001; Wald and Link, 2002; Freeman et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2001; Wald and Link, 2002; Freeman et al., 2006.

claim: The prevalence of HSV-2 in sub-Saharan Africa is approximately 70%.
source: The extremely high prevalence of HSV-2 in sub-Saharan Africa (∼70%) (Looker et al., 2008) may contribute more to the spread of HIV-1 than number of sex partners or other sexually transmitted infections (Freeman et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Looker et al., 2008.

claim: HSV establishes latency in neurons with frequent subclinical or clinical reactivations.
source: Moreover, as HSV establishes latency in neurons with frequent subclinical or clinical reactivations, there is a lifelong impact of infection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HSV biology.

claim: HSV-1 has emerged as a predominant cause of genital disease in the developed world.
source: Notably, HSV-1 has emerged as a predominant cause of genital disease in the developed world (Roberts et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2006; Horowitz et al., 2011; Bernstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2006; Horowitz et al., 2011; Bernstein et al., 2013.

claim: An HSV-2 gD adjuvanted subunit vaccine provided no protection against HSV-2 genital disease.
source: For example, in the most recent efficacy trial, an HSV-2 gD adjuvanted subunit vaccine provided no protection against HSV-2 genital disease, but surprisingly provided 35% cross-protection against HSV-1 infection and 58% cross-protection against HSV-1 disease (Belshe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belshe et al., 2012.

claim: An HSV-2 gD adjuvanted subunit vaccine provided 35% cross-protection against HSV-1 infection.
source: For example, in the most recent efficacy trial, an HSV-2 gD adjuvanted subunit vaccine provided no protection against HSV-2 genital disease, but surprisingly provided 35% cross-protection against HSV-1 infection and 58% cross-protection against HSV-1 disease (Belshe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belshe et al., 2012.

claim: An HSV-2 gD adjuvanted subunit vaccine provided 58% cross-protection against HSV-1 disease.
source: For example, in the most recent efficacy trial, an HSV-2 gD adjuvanted subunit vaccine provided no protection against HSV-2 genital disease, but surprisingly provided 35% cross-protection against HSV-1 infection and 58% cross-protection against HSV-1 disease (Belshe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belshe et al., 2012.

claim: The gD-2 subunit vaccine elicited CD4+, but not CD8+ T cell responses.
source: The gD-2 subunit vaccine also elicited CD4+, but not CD8+ T cell responses; however, the cellular responses did not correlate with HSV-1 protection (Belshe et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belshe et al., 2014.

claim: The cellular responses elicited by the gD-2 subunit vaccine did not correlate with HSV-1 protection.
source: The gD-2 subunit vaccine also elicited CD4+, but not CD8+ T cell responses; however, the cellular responses did not correlate with HSV-1 protection (Belshe et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Belshe et al., 2014.

claim: HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 replicates in VD60 cells to high titers.
source: The HSV-1 gD complemented HSV-2 mutant virus (designated HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1) replicates in VD60 cells to high titers, but a single passage through non-complementing cells yields non-infectious progeny, reflecting the requirement for gD in entry and cell-to-cell spread.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data described in the Results section showing the virus grew to 10^8 pfu/ml on VD60 cells.

claim: A single passage of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 through non-complementing cells yields non-infectious progeny.
source: The HSV-1 gD complemented HSV-2 mutant virus (designated HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1) replicates in VD60 cells to high titers, but a single passage through non-complementing cells yields non-infectious progeny, reflecting the requirement for gD in entry and cell-to-cell spread.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no plaques were observed when virus grown on VD60 cells was plated on Vero cells.

claim: gD is required for viral entry and cell-to-cell spread.
source: The HSV-1 gD complemented HSV-2 mutant virus (designated HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1) replicates in VD60 cells to high titers, but a single passage through non-complementing cells yields non-infectious progeny, reflecting the requirement for gD in entry and cell-to-cell spread.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about gD function.

claim: HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 grew to high titers (10^8 pfu/ml) when phenotypically complemented by growing on VD60 cells.
source: The virus was subsequently subjected to three rounds of plaque purification and grew to high titers (108 pfu/ml) when phenotypically complemented by growing the virus on VD60 cells, which express HSV-1 gD under the control of the gD-1 promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on virus propagation.

claim: No plaques were observed when three independent plaque-purified isolates of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 grown to 10^8 pfu on VD60 cells were plated on non-complementing Vero cells.
source: No plaques were observed when three independent plaque-purified isolates were grown to 108 pfu on VD60 cells and then plated on non-complementing Vero cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data demonstrating the virus cannot replicate without complementation.

claim: No recombinants were detected by PCR in HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1.
source: Moreover, no recombinants were detected by PCR, most likely reflecting differences in the regions flanking gD in VD60 cells and in HSV-2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PCR analysis.

claim: The lack of recombinants in HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 reflects differences in the regions flanking gD in VD60 cells and in HSV-2.
source: Moreover, no recombinants were detected by PCR, most likely reflecting differences in the regions flanking gD in VD60 cells and in HSV-2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 and ΔgD−/− show similar levels of expression of other HSV viral proteins when grown on VD60 or Vero cells.
source: Western blots show similar levels of expression of other HSV viral proteins when the deletion virus is grown on VD60 or Vero cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SCID mice inoculated intravaginally with 10^7 pfu of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 manifested no signs of disease.
source: SCID mice inoculated intravaginally with 107 pfu of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 manifested no signs of disease, whereas animals inoculated with 104 pfu of HSV-2(G) quickly succumbed to the infection and manifested severe HSV-2-induced epithelial and neurological disease (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: SCID mice inoculated intravaginally with 10^4 pfu of HSV-2(G) quickly succumbed to the infection and manifested severe HSV-2-induced epithelial and neurological disease.
source: SCID mice inoculated intravaginally with 107 pfu of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 manifested no signs of disease, whereas animals inoculated with 104 pfu of HSV-2(G) quickly succumbed to the infection and manifested severe HSV-2-induced epithelial and neurological disease (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Subcutaneous inoculation with wild-type HSV-2 virus induced disease (60% mortality with 10^5 pfu) in SCID mice.
source: Subcutaneous inoculation with wild-type virus also induced disease (60% mortality with 105 pfu), while no evidence of disease was observed following exposure to high doses of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 in SCID mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No evidence of disease was observed in SCID mice following exposure to high doses of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1.
source: Subcutaneous inoculation with wild-type virus also induced disease (60% mortality with 105 pfu), while no evidence of disease was observed following exposure to high doses of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 in SCID mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No virus was detected in the neural tissue of SCID mice inoculated intravaginally with HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 by qPCR.
source: Moreover, no virus was detected in the neural tissue of SCID mice inoculated intravaginally with HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 by qPCR (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The majority of vaccinated mice (14/20) showed no evidence of epithelial disease after intravaginal challenge.
source: The majority of the vaccinated mice (14/20) showed no evidence of epithelial disease (Figure 3B) and none showed any signs of neurological disease (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: None of the vaccinated mice showed any signs of neurological disease after intravaginal challenge.
source: The majority of the vaccinated mice (14/20) showed no evidence of epithelial disease (Figure 3B) and none showed any signs of neurological disease (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HSV was detected by plaque assay in vaginal washes from vaccinated mice only on day 2 post-challenge but was cleared by day 4 post-challenge.
source: The mice with epithelial signs recovered fully and HSV was detected by plaque assay in vaginal washes from vaccinated mice only on day 2 post–challenge but was cleared by day 4 post–challenge (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No infectious virus was recovered from vaginal or neural tissue in HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD-1-vaccinated mice at day 5 post-infection.
source: Moreover, no infectious virus was recovered from vaginal or neural tissue in HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD-1-vaccinated mice at day 5 post-infection, but virus was readily detected from all of these sites in control-vaccinated mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Virus was readily detected from vaginal and neural tissue in control-vaccinated mice at day 5 post-infection.
source: Moreover, no infectious virus was recovered from vaginal or neural tissue in HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD-1-vaccinated mice at day 5 post-infection, but virus was readily detected from all of these sites in control-vaccinated mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No virus could be reactivated from dorsal root ganglia cultured ex vivo for 21 days from vaccinated mice.
source: Furthermore, we were unable to reactivate any virus from dorsal root ganglia (DRG) cultured ex vivo for 21 days (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: Virus reactivated from DRG extracted from all control-vaccinated animals.
source: In contrast, virus reactivated from DRG extracted from all control-vaccinated animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: HSV DNA (US6 gene) was not detected by qPCR in vaccinated mice (limit of detection 3 HSV-2 genome copies).
source: In addition, HSV DNA (US6 gene) was not detected by qPCR in vaccinated mice (limit of detection 3 HSV-2 genome copies), but was detected in all controls (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: HSV DNA (US6 gene) was detected by qPCR in all control-vaccinated mice.
source: In addition, HSV DNA (US6 gene) was not detected by qPCR in vaccinated mice (limit of detection 3 HSV-2 genome copies), but was detected in all controls (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The vaccine protected 100% of mice independent of hormonal treatment with MPA.
source: The vaccine protected 100% of mice independent of hormonal treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 100% of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated BALB/c mice survived intravaginal challenge.
source: Consistent with the findings in C57BL/6 mice, 100% of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice survived intravaginal challenge (Figure 3I) and no infectious virus or viral DNA was recovered from neural tissues at day 7 and 21 post-infection (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: No infectious virus or viral DNA was recovered from neural tissues of vaccinated BALB/c mice at day 7 and 21 post-infection.
source: Consistent with the findings in C57BL/6 mice, 100% of HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice survived intravaginal challenge (Figure 3I) and no infectious virus or viral DNA was recovered from neural tissues at day 7 and 21 post-infection (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Control-vaccinated mice developed zosteriform lesions, neurologic disease and succumbed to infection following challenge with HSV-2 in the skin scarification model.
source: The control-vaccinated (VD60 lysate) mice developed zosteriform lesions, neurologic disease and succumbed to infection following challenge with HSV-2, whereas HSV-1 produced more modest signs (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: HSV-1 produced more modest signs than HSV-2 in control-vaccinated mice in the skin scarification model.
source: The control-vaccinated (VD60 lysate) mice developed zosteriform lesions, neurologic disease and succumbed to infection following challenge with HSV-2, whereas HSV-1 produced more modest signs (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice showed minimal signs of epithelial disease (maximal disease score 1) in the skin scarification model.
source: More importantly, the HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice showed minimal signs of epithelial disease (maximal disease score 1), no neurological signs and 100% survival after challenge with either serotype (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice showed no neurological signs in the skin scarification model.
source: More importantly, the HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice showed minimal signs of epithelial disease (maximal disease score 1), no neurological signs and 100% survival after challenge with either serotype (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice showed 100% survival after skin challenge with either HSV-1 or HSV-2.
source: More importantly, the HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice showed minimal signs of epithelial disease (maximal disease score 1), no neurological signs and 100% survival after challenge with either serotype (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No HSV was detected by titering or qPCR in day 14 skin biopsies or neural tissue from HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice in the skin scarification model.
source: No HSV was detected by titering or qPCR in day 14 skin biopsies or neural tissue from HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice; whereas virus was detected in 100% of control mice challenged with HSV-2 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Virus was detected in 100% of control mice challenged with HSV-2 in the skin scarification model.
source: No HSV was detected by titering or qPCR in day 14 skin biopsies or neural tissue from HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice; whereas virus was detected in 100% of control mice challenged with HSV-2 (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Mice treated with a single dose of immune serum displayed modest epithelial signs (mean score 2) after intravaginal challenge.
source: Mice treated with a single dose of immune serum displayed modest epithelial signs (mean score 2), but no neurologic disease with 100% survival (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Mice treated with a single dose of immune serum showed no neurologic disease with 100% survival after intravaginal challenge.
source: Mice treated with a single dose of immune serum displayed modest epithelial signs (mean score 2), but no neurologic disease with 100% survival (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Mice that received T cells from immune mice or serum or T cells from controls succumbed to disease after intravaginal challenge.
source: In contrast, mice that received T cells from immune mice or serum or T cells from the controls succumbed to disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Depletion of immunoglobulins from the immune serum by passage on a Protein L column abolished the protective capacity.
source: Depletion of immunoglobulins from the immune serum by passage on a Protein L column abolished the protective capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HSV-specific Abs were detected in vaginal washes in mice that received the immune, but not control serum.
source: HSV-specific Abs were detected in vaginal washes in mice that received the immune, but not control serum (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Immune sera treated mice survived skin challenge.
source: Intraperitoneal administration of serum also protected mice from skin disease. The immune sera treated mice survived challenge (Figure 5C) and developed moderate signs of epithelial disease (mean score of 2.2), which peaked on day 6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Immune sera treated mice developed moderate signs of epithelial disease (mean score of 2.2) in the skin challenge model, which peaked on day 6.
source: Intraperitoneal administration of serum also protected mice from skin disease. The immune sera treated mice survived challenge (Figure 5C) and developed moderate signs of epithelial disease (mean score of 2.2), which peaked on day 6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No neurological signs were observed in immune sera treated mice in the skin challenge model.
source: Moreover, no neurological signs were observed and no virus was detected in neural tissue by titering or qPCR (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data described in the text.

claim: No virus was detected in neural tissue by titering or qPCR in immune sera treated mice in the skin challenge model.
source: Moreover, no neurological signs were observed and no virus was detected in neural tissue by titering or qPCR (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Mice that received control serum developed severe epithelial and neurological disease and succumbed to the infection with 100% lethality in the skin challenge model.
source: In contrast, mice that received control serum developed severe epithelial and neurological disease and succumbed to the infection with 100% lethality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HSV-specific Ab responses were consistently observed with serum dilutions as high as 1:800,000 at 7 days post-boost.
source: HSV-specific Ab responses were consistently observed with serum dilutions as high as 1:800,000 7 days post-boost (Figure 6A) and were detected in vaginal washes within 4 days of challenge, indicating transport of HSV Abs into the vaginal lumen (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HSV-specific Abs were detected in vaginal washes within 4 days of challenge, indicating transport of HSV Abs into the vaginal lumen.
source: HSV-specific Ab responses were consistently observed with serum dilutions as high as 1:800,000 7 days post-boost (Figure 6A) and were detected in vaginal washes within 4 days of challenge, indicating transport of HSV Abs into the vaginal lumen (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The serum HSV-specific Abs exhibited low levels of neutralizing activity (1:5 dilution).
source: The serum HSV-specific Abs exhibited low levels of neutralizing activity (1:5 dilution) (Figure 6C), but did display ADCC activity, which was reduced in the presence of anti-FcγR Ab (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The serum HSV-specific Abs displayed ADCC activity, which was reduced in the presence of anti-FcγR Ab.
source: The serum HSV-specific Abs exhibited low levels of neutralizing activity (1:5 dilution) (Figure 6C), but did display ADCC activity, which was reduced in the presence of anti-FcγR Ab (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The HSV-specific Abs in serum and vaginal washes were comprised predominantly of IgG2a and IgG2b.
source: The HSV-specific Abs in serum and vaginal washes were comprised predominantly of IgG2a and IgG2b (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and recognized multiple viral proteins on Western blots with HSV-2-infected cell lysates as the immunogen (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The HSV-specific Abs recognized multiple viral proteins on Western blots with HSV-2-infected cell lysates as the immunogen.
source: The HSV-specific Abs in serum and vaginal washes were comprised predominantly of IgG2a and IgG2b (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and recognized multiple viral proteins on Western blots with HSV-2-infected cell lysates as the immunogen (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Serum from control-immunized and subsequently HSV-2 infected mice recognized a more restricted set of proteins compared to ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice.
source: Serum from control-immunized and subsequently HSV-2 infected mice (obtained at day 8 post–challenge) recognized a more restricted set of proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The predominant antigen recognized by control-immunized, HSV-2-challenged, but not ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice, is gD.
source: Western blots with purified HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 or HSV-2 ΔgD−/− indicate that the predominant antigen recognized by control-immunized, HSV-2-challenged, but not ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated mice, is gD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ∼100 kDa band recognized by the ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated immune serum is gB.
source: Blots with recombinant glycoprotein B-1 identify the ∼100 kDa band recognized by the ΔgD−/+gD−1-vaccinated immune serum as gB (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HSV-specific Abs were detected in vaginal washes of the FcγR−/− mice but failed to provide protection.
source: HSV-specific Abs were detected in vaginal washes of the FcγR−/− mice, but failed to provide protection, whereas Abs were not detected in vaginal washes from FcRn−/− mice consistent with the role of FcRn in transport of Abs from serum to the mucosa (Li et al., 2011) (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Abs were not detected in vaginal washes from FcRn−/− mice consistent with the role of FcRn in transport of Abs from serum to the mucosa.
source: HSV-specific Abs were detected in vaginal washes of the FcγR−/− mice, but failed to provide protection, whereas Abs were not detected in vaginal washes from FcRn−/− mice consistent with the role of FcRn in transport of Abs from serum to the mucosa (Li et al., 2011) (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D and a citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Deletion of gD may unmask viral antigens important in generating a protective humoral response.
source: Possibly, deletion of gD, which is immunodominant as evidenced by the immune response in control, HSV-2 challenged mice (Figure 6F) and by clinical data showing that the majority of HSV-infected individuals have neutralizing Abs to gD (Cairns et al., 2014), unmasks viral antigens important in generating a protective humoral response.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the data and cited literature.

claim: gD is immunodominant as evidenced by the immune response in control, HSV-2 challenged mice.
source: Possibly, deletion of gD, which is immunodominant as evidenced by the immune response in control, HSV-2 challenged mice (Figure 6F) and by clinical data showing that the majority of HSV-infected individuals have neutralizing Abs to gD (Cairns et al., 2014), unmasks viral antigens important in generating a protective humoral response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The majority of HSV-infected individuals have neutralizing Abs to gD.
source: Possibly, deletion of gD, which is immunodominant as evidenced by the immune response in control, HSV-2 challenged mice (Figure 6F) and by clinical data showing that the majority of HSV-infected individuals have neutralizing Abs to gD (Cairns et al., 2014), unmasks viral antigens important in generating a protective humoral response.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cairns et al., 2014.

claim: gD may modulate immune responses through its interactions with herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM) on immune cells.
source: Additionally, gD may modulate immune responses through its interactions with herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM) on immune cells (La et al., 2002; Aubert et al., 2009; Stiles et al., 2010; Kopp et al., 2012; Grauwet et al., 2014; Sharma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In the absence of the gD-HVEM interaction, the host may mount a polyantigenic IgG2 dominant response capable of eliciting FcR-mediated protection.
source: Interactions between gD and HVEM may skew the immune response towards neutralizing Abs whereas in the absence of the gD-HVEM interaction or yet undiscovered immunosuppressive functions of gD, the host may mount a polyantigenic IgG2 dominant response capable of eliciting FcR-mediated protection.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Heat-killed HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 failed to protect mice from vaginal challenge.
source: Consistent with this is the observation that heat-killed HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 failed to protect mice from vaginal challenge (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data mentioned but not shown.

claim: The flanking regions of gD in HSV-1 and HSV-2 share approximately 54% and 73% identity within the 5′ and 3′ region of the US6 gene, respectively.
source: The flanking regions of gD in HSV-1 and HSV-2 share approximately 54% and 73% identity within the 5′ and 3′ region of the US6 gene, respectively (HSV-1(KOS) vs HSV-2(HG52), NCBI genome, Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The level of homology between HSV-1 and HSV-2 flanking regions of gD makes recombination highly unlikely.
source: This level of homology makes recombination highly unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence homology data.

claim: The gH deletion viral vaccine did not prevent the establishment of latency in mice.
source: Unlike the data presented here with the HSV-2 ΔgD virus, the gH deletion viral vaccine did not prevent the establishment of latency in mice (Speck et al., 1996), was not shown to passively transfer protection and failed to reduce recurrences when evaluated as a therapeutic vaccine in a clinical trial (de Bruyn et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Speck et al., 1996 and de Bruyn et al., 2006.

claim: The gH deletion viral vaccine was not shown to passively transfer protection.

evidence: This claim is stated as a fact about the gH deletion vaccine.

source: This deletion virus also differs from the HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 vaccine candidate described here in that it does not induce as high an Ab response, has not been shown to passively protect, and did not prevent the establishment of latency as low levels of viral DNA were detected in the DRG following both immunization and viral challenge (Hoshino et al., 2005, 2008, 2009; Dudek et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: Protection following immunization with tk-deletion viruses requires anti-HSV-2 T cells in the genital tract.
source: Protection following immunization with tk-deletion viruses requires anti-HSV-2 T cells in the genital tract (Milligan et al., 2004; Shin and Iwasaki, 2012) and serum from mice immunized with this tk-deletion virus has not been shown to passively transfer protection (Morrison et al., 2001; Milligan et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Milligan et al., 2004; Shin and Iwasaki, 2012.

claim: Serum from mice immunized with tk-deletion virus has not been shown to passively transfer protection.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morrison et al., 2001; Milligan et al., 2004.

claim: Non-neutralizing antibodies that mediate ADCC and antibody-mediated phagocytosis contributed to protection against HIV in the RV144 vaccine trial.
source: Consistent with this concept are the results of the HIV RV144 vaccine trial, which found that non-neutralizing antibodies that mediate ADCC and antibody-mediated phagocytosis contributed to protection against HIV (Bonsignori et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bonsignori et al., 2012.

claim: Ab–FcγR interactions are required to mediate protection against influenza.
source: Moreover, recent studies suggest that Ab–FcγR interactions are required to mediate protection against influenza (Dilillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dilillo et al., 2014.

claim: The HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 vaccine may be an ideal vaccine vector for other pathogens that enter through mucosal sites.
source: Together these findings suggest that the HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 vaccine provides a model to elicit such protective responses and indicate that it may be an ideal vaccine vector for other pathogens that enter through these sites.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the results.

claim: By deleting the gene for gD, which is required for cell-to-cell spread, the cells initially infected by the complemented virus may function as a 'factory' generating viral proteins and 'defective' particles that are immunogenic.
source: An additional mechanism that may contribute to the protection observed with the HSV-2 ΔgD−/+gD−1 vaccine and to the observation that it induces Abs to multiple viral proteins is that by deleting the gene for gD, which is required for cell-to-cell spread, the cells initially infected by the complemented virus may function as a 'factory' generating viral proteins and 'defective' particles that are immunogenic.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the mechanism of action.

claim: The vaginal wash Abs were predominantly IgG, not IgA.
source: Notably, the vaginal wash Abs were predominantly IgG, not IgA (data not shown), which is consistent with prior studies that have shown that while the predominant immunoglobulin by weight in the vaginal mucus of immune mice is secretory IgA, HSV-specific Abs are almost entirely IgG (Parr and Parr, 1998; Parr et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (not shown) and citations to Parr and Parr, 1998; Parr et al., 1998.
